propositions.text: The appellants are Hungarian citizens appealing the RPD's denial of refugee protection.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (principal Appellant), his spouse XXXX XXXX and their minor children XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX, (minor Appellants) who claim to be citizens of the Republic of Hungary , appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: No new evidence was submitted in support of the appeal.
propositions.quote: They have submitted no new evidence in support of their appeal.

propositions.text: The principal appellant remains the designated representative for her child under RAD Rule 23(1).
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant has remained the designated representative (DR) for her child and is deemed to continue for the RAD appeal under RAD Rule 23(1).

propositions.text: The appellants ask the RAD to overturn the RPD decision and find them refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to overturn the decision of the RPD and to find that the Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Alternatively, appellants request a new hearing before a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the Appellants request that the matter be returned to the RPD for a new hearing under a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants, Hungarian citizens, appeal the RPD's denial without new evidence, seeking refugee status or a new hearing; the principal appellant remains representative.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD's decision that the appellants are neither Convention Refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention Refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD's decision denying refugee protection to the appellants under IRPA section 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The appellants fear returning to Hungary due to discrimination and persecution based on Roma ethnicity.
propositions.quote: The Appellants fear returning to Hungary because they allege that, on account of their Roma ethnicity, they have been discriminated and persecuted.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants allege fear of persecution in Hungary due to their Roma ethnicity.

propositions.text: The RPD heard the appellants' refugee claim on August 24, 2015, and rejected it on September 15, 2015.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' refugee claim was heard on August 24, 2015. The RPD in written decision issued on September 15, 2015 rejected their claims

propositions.text: The RPD found the appellants not credible and that state protection was available.
propositions.quote: finding that the Appellants were not credible and that state protection was available to them.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the appellants' claim in 2015, finding them not credible and state protection available.

propositions.text: IRPA sets grounds and remedies for appeal but does not specify the RAD's standard of review.
propositions.quote: While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.

paragraphs.summary: IRPA provides appeal grounds and remedies but not the RAD's review standard, says the court.

propositions.text: Appellant's counsel made submissions on the RAD's role in reviewing RPD decisions.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's counsel has made submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of an RPD decision.

propositions.text: The Federal Court decision in Huruglica guides the RAD's standard of review as a hybrid appeal requiring independent assessment.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision, in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal.

propositions.text: Huruglica requires the RAD to conduct a hybrid appeal, independently assessing refugee status and substituting its decision if it departs from the RPD.
propositions.quote: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.

propositions.text: The RAD may respect RPD credibility findings but is not limited to intervening only for overriding errors.
propositions.quote: [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."

paragraphs.summary: Appellant counsel submitted on RAD's role; court finds Huruglica requires RAD to conduct hybrid appeal with independent assessment, respecting but not bound by RPD credibility findings.

propositions.text: The RAD will independently assess the RPD decision, respecting credibility findings where RPD has advantage.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The RAD will recognize and respect the credibility findings of the RPD or other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will independently assess the RPD decision, respecting credibility findings where RPD has advantage, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD adopts reasoning from RAD Member Bosveld on the RAD's role and deference to RPD findings.
propositions.quote: In a decision issued by RAD Member Edward Bosveld, which I adopt and accept his reasoning, Member Bosveld considered at some length the legislation and jurisprudence concerning the role of the RAD.

propositions.text: Bosveld's conclusions on RAD appeals and deference to RPD findings apply here.
propositions.quote: The panel reached the following conclusions, which it finds to also be applicable here, about the approach to be taken in a RAD appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD adopts Member Bosveld's reasoning on RAD's role and deference to RPD findings as applicable here.

propositions.text: The RAD will assess all evidence, including RPD record and admissible new evidence, and consider law, fact, and mixed questions raised by parties.
propositions.quote: The RAD will take the following approach in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD. It will assess all of the evidence, both that in the RPD's record and any admissible new evidence. It will consider questions of law, fact, and mixed law and fact which was raised by the Appellant and, where applicable, the Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will assess all evidence and consider legal and factual questions raised by parties, says the court.

propositions.text: In a true appeal with no new evidence, the RAD reviews the RPD decision and determines if it is wrong by independent assessment.
propositions.quote: Where the proceeding is a true appeal-that is, where there is no admissible new evidence, as is the case here-the RAD will consider the decision of the RPD, the submissions in respect of that decision, and determine whether the RPD's determination is wrong. As a true appeal is founded on the record, the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of the evidence in that record in order to determine the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: For true appeals without new evidence, the RAD independently assesses the RPD decision to determine if it is wrong.

propositions.text: If new evidence shows error in RPD decision, the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal considering RPD reasons and new evidence.
propositions.quote: Where an appeal includes admissible new evidence that speaks to an error in the RPD's decision, it is a hybrid appeal, where the RAD must consider the RPD's reasons in light of the new evidence, which may establish that the decision of the RPD is wrong.

paragraphs.summary: If new evidence shows error, the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal considering RPD reasons and new evidence.

propositions.text: New evidence establishing changed risk leads to limited de novo appeal; RAD considers RPD record but new evidence may be determinative.
propositions.quote: Where an appeal presents admissible new evidence which establishes a new, changed, or heightened risk, or otherwise changes the overall nature of the claim, this will result in a limited de novo appeal. In some such cases, the decision of the RPD may be less relevant in light of the new evidence-that is, the new evidence establishes a risk or degree of risk, or other potentially determinative matter not considered by the RPD. Unlike a true de novo proceed, however, the RAD will not ignore the RPD's record or the findings of the lower tribunal, as these may remain relevant to the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: New evidence showing changed risk leads to limited de novo appeal; RAD considers RPD record but new evidence may be determinative.

propositions.text: RAD respects RPD findings where RPD had advantage, usually credibility and fact findings, and intervenes only if reasoning is incomprehensible or unsupported.
propositions.quote: The RAD will recognize and respect findings which the RPD was in an advantageous position to make, which will normally include credibility findings and other findings of fact. Where such deference is to be shown, the RAD will not intervene unless the RPD's reasoning process is not comprehensible or the outcome of that process is not based on and supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: RAD defers to RPD findings where RPD had advantage, intervening only if reasoning is incomprehensible or unsupported.

propositions.text: Where RPD's decision is based on findings warranting deference, RAD assesses if reasoning is comprehensible and evidence-based.
propositions.quote: Where the RPD's determination is entirely based on findings which warrant deference-such as an overall lack of credibility, based on oral testimony-the RAD will, having conducted its own assessment of the evidence, consider whether the RPD's reasoning process is comprehensible and whether the determination is based on and supported by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: If RPD's decision rests on findings warranting deference, RAD checks if reasoning is comprehensible and supported by evidence.

propositions.text: On matters where RPD has no advantage, RAD applies correctness standard and substitutes or refers back if it disagrees.
propositions.quote: On matters where the RPD has no advantage, the RAD will show no deference and will apply a standard of correctness, engaging in its own analysis of the evidence and reaching its own conclusion to determine if the RPD was wrong. Where the RAD finds that its conclusion does not agree with that of the RPD, the RAD will substitute its own finding and determination or, if it is unable to substitute, will refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: Where RPD has no advantage, RAD applies correctness standard and substitutes or refers back if it disagrees.

propositions.text: The appellants request an oral hearing under IRPA section 110(6).
propositions.quote: The Appellants requests an oral hearing pursuant to Section 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants request an oral hearing under IRPA section 110(6).

propositions.text: Section 110(3) requires RAD to proceed without hearing on RPD record but allows documentary evidence and submissions.
propositions.quote: Section 110(3) of IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD's record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) allows appellant to present only evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available before.
propositions.quote: The person who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to Section 110(4), present "only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection."

paragraphs.summary: Section 110(3) requires RAD to proceed without hearing on RPD record but allows documentary evidence; section 110(4) limits appellant's evidence to new or unavailable evidence.

propositions.text: Section 110(6) allows RAD to hold hearing if new documentary evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision.
propositions.quote: According to Section 110(6), upon which the Appellants rely, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: In this appeal, documentary evidence under 110(3) must be understood in relation to 110(4) due to no Minister evidence.
propositions.quote: In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

paragraphs.summary: Section 110(6) allows hearing if new documentary evidence raises serious credibility issue central to RPD decision; here, 110(3) evidence must be read with 110(4).

propositions.text: Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) together mean RAD must not hold hearing without new evidence raising serious credibility issue central to RPD decision.
propositions.quote: When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) require new evidence raising serious credibility issue to hold hearing; otherwise no hearing.

propositions.text: Appellants submitted no new evidence; RAD must proceed without hearing and denies oral hearing request.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not submitted new evidence in support of their appeal. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing in their appeal, and their application for an oral hearing is denied.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants submitted no new evidence; RAD proceeds without hearing and denies oral hearing request.

propositions.text: The RPD found the determinative issues are credibility and failure to rebut presumption of state protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the determinative issues in this claim are credibility, and that the Appellants had not rebutted the presumption of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility and state protection presumption issues determinative in the claim.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue the RPD erred in credibility findings and that no state protection exists in Hungary.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its credibility findings and that there is no state protection for them in Hungary.

propositions.text: The RAD will decide the appeal based on state protection issue, not credibility except as it relates to state protection.
propositions.quote: As the issue of state protection is sufficient to dispose of this appeal, however, it is not necessary for the RAD to consider the Appellant's arguments in respect of credibility, other than those that relate to the RPD's analysis of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue RPD erred on credibility and state protection; RAD will focus on state protection issue.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant arrived in Canada April 23, 2015, denied entry, returned to Hungary, and did not claim refugee protection then.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (principal Appellant), arrived to Canada on April 23, 2015 to visit family, however, he was denied entry after failing to establish that he was a visitor to Canada and returned to Hungary.

propositions.text: RPD questioned why no refugee claim was made at that time.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned why he did not make a claim for refugee protection at that time.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified he came alone due to financial constraints and was told by immigration official to return with family and was refused refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant testified that he came to visit family and that due to financial restrains he did not bring his family...the principal Appellant testified that he did want to file a claim but was refused by the official and told to return to Hungary, and come back to Canada with his family, the official told him to leave the country.

propositions.text: RPD did not find principal Appellant's explanation and testimony credible.
propositions.quote: The RPD gave fulsome reasoning as to why it did not find his explanation and testimony credible.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the principal Appellant's testimony about denied refugee claim in 2015 not credible.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the principal Appellant's explanation somewhat disingenuous and not credible.
propositions.quote: The RAD found this explanation to be "somewhat disingenuous" because the principal Appellant's testimony just didn't make sense.

propositions.text: Appellant's counsel stated principal Appellant came alone to visit family and to make refugee claim but was refused.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's own counsel put on the record that the principal Appellant had come to Canada alone to visit family, but also to make a refugee claim but was refused.

propositions.text: RPD found it not credible that officer denied refugee claim because claimant lacked family; officers presumed to act regularly.
propositions.quote: To infer that an officer denied acceptance of the claim as the claimant did not have his family is not credible...public officials at the port of entry benefit from the presumption of bureaucratic regularity.

propositions.text: RPD found claimant did not seek refugee protection in April 2015 as alleged.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant did not seek refugee protection in April 2015 as he alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with RPD that the principal Appellant's claim of being denied refugee claim in 2015 is not credible.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant argues RPD wrongly accused him of disingenuous evidence about failure to seek protection in 2015.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant argues that the RPD wrongly accused him of giving disingenuous evidence about his failure to seek protection upon arrival in Canada on April 2015.

propositions.text: RAD finds it reasonable for RPD to expect refugee claim at airport in 2015 and no error in RPD's finding.
propositions.quote: In the RAD's view, it was reasonable for the RPD to expect the Appellant to have sought protection by filing a refugee claim at the Airport upon arrival in 2015, and finds no error in the RPD's finding in this regard.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant returned to Hungary and lived at same address where he alleged persecution until July 2015.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant returned to Hungary and continued to live at the same address until his departure in July 2015.

propositions.text: This undermines his subjective fear and contradicts his explanation for coming alone due to financial constraints.
propositions.quote: This was the same area where he alleged he was persecuted; the RAD finds, this certainly brings his subjective fear into question...This also runs contrary to his explanation of why he originally came alone to Canada due to financial constraints.

propositions.text: RAD accepts RPD's credibility finding that principal Appellant's explanation does not make sense.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that his explanation just plainly doesn't make sense and accepts the credibility finding of the RPD in this area.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no error in RPD's credibility finding and notes contradictions in principal Appellant's explanations.

propositions.text: Adult Appellants testified at RPD hearing; RAD reviewed hearing recording.
propositions.quote: In this particular appeal, the adult Appellants provided oral testimony at the RPD hearing and the RAD has had an opportunity to listen to the recording of the RPD hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The adult Appellants testified at RPD hearing and RAD reviewed the recording.

propositions.text: Female adult Appellant testified she was verbally and physically assaulted by guards at school in early 2014 and suffered bruises and inability to stand.
propositions.quote: In her testimony, XXXX XXXX stated that one day in January or February 2014, that whilst she had gone to pick up her child at school, she was attacked by a group of guards. They verbally and physically assaulted her and she suffered bruises and was unable to stand as a result of the physical assault.

propositions.text: RPD asked if she sought medical attention; she said no because she believed she would not get it.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked the female adult Appellant if she sought medical attention. The female adult Appellant testified that she did not seek medical attention, as she believed she would not get medical attention.

propositions.text: RPD had credibility concerns about her failure to seek medical attention.
propositions.quote: The RPD had credibility concerns with respect to the fact that the Appellant had not sought medical attention for her injuries.

paragraphs.summary: The female adult Appellant testified to assault and no medical attention; RPD had credibility concerns about this.

propositions.text: RPD asked if female adult Appellant filed police complaint; she said no because police do not help Roma.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked the female adult Appellant if she had filed a complaint with the police. The female adult Appellant testified that she did not file a report with the police because the police do not help the Roma.

propositions.text: RAD finds RPD's finding supportable; difference between being refused and failing to seek medical treatment.
propositions.quote: The RAD after reviewing the evidence in this area, finds the RPD finding to be supportable. There is a difference between being refused medical treatment and seeking medical treatment, in this case the female adult Appellant failed to seek medical treatment and the RAD finds there is no evidence to the contrary.

paragraphs.summary: The female adult Appellant did not file police complaint; RAD supports RPD finding on medical treatment failure.

propositions.text: No evidence that principal Appellant was denied protection due to Roma ethnicity.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence before the RAD panel to indicate that principal Appellant was denied protection because of his Roma ethnicity.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence shows principal Appellant was denied protection due to Roma ethnicity.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant mentioned incidents of discrimination due to Roma ethnicity in BOC form.
propositions.quote: In his Basis of Claim (BOC) form, principal Appellant mentions a number of other incidents where he alleges he suffered discrimination on account of his Roma ethnicity.

propositions.text: RPD asked when he first contacted police about discrimination; he said April 2015.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked him when was the first time that he ever contacted the police to complain about the alleged discrimination and he stated that it was in April 2015.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Appellant alleged discrimination incidents but first police contact was April 2015.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant did not report incidents before 2015 and did not alert police reasonably.
propositions.quote: Based on the testimony of principal Appellant, the RAD finds that he did not report any of the incidents mentioned in his BOC form which took place prior to 2015...he did not do everything that he reasonably could, to alert the police or to provide information to them.

propositions.text: To qualify for refugee status, claimant must show they sought but could not obtain state protection or state could not be expected to provide it.
propositions.quote: To qualify for refugee status, an Appellant must satisfy the Board that he or she sought, but was unable to obtain, protection from their home state, or alternatively, that their home state, on an objective basis, could not be expected to provide protection.

propositions.text: Adequacy of state protection is assessed objectively, not based on applicant's reluctance to seek it.
propositions.quote: The adequacy of state protection...cannot be assessed on the basis of the Applicant's reluctance or failure to seek it...if the state can, objectively speaking, provide adequate protection...then she has not rebutted the basic presumption that state protection is available to her.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds principal Appellant failed to report incidents and must show objective lack of state protection to qualify as refugee.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant gave no sound reason for failure to report; failure to pursue state protection is fatal to claim in functioning democracy.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that principal Appellant has provided no sound rational for his failure to report these incidents...a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy...

paragraphs.summary: Failure to report incidents without good reason is fatal to refugee claim in functioning democracy, RAD finds.

propositions.text: Other alleged discrimination incidents do not rise to level of persecution.
propositions.quote: All of the adult Appellants testified as to other incidents in which they allege they were discriminated against but, the RAD concludes that these do not rise to the level of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: RAD concludes other alleged discrimination incidents do not amount to persecution.

propositions.text: RAD is guided by Supreme Court, Federal Court of Appeal and Federal Court jurisprudence on state protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by the jurisprudence from the Supreme Court of Canada, the Federal Court of Appeal and the Federal Court.

paragraphs.summary: RAD applies Supreme Court and Federal Court jurisprudence on state protection.

propositions.text: Ward decision presumes state protection unless clear and convincing evidence shows state's inability to protect.
propositions.quote: The presumption of state protection was articulated by the Supreme Court of Canada in the Ward decision where the Court stated:...Absent some evidence, the claim should fail, as nations should be presumed capable of protecting their citizens.

paragraphs.summary: Ward decision presumes state protection unless clear evidence shows state's inability to protect, court explains.

propositions.text: Ward established onus on Appellants to produce clear and convincing evidence that state cannot provide protection.
propositions.quote: Ward has established that the onus is on the Appellants to produce clear and convincing evidence that the state cannot provide protection.

paragraphs.summary: Ward requires Appellants to produce clear and convincing evidence of state's inability to protect.

propositions.text: Hungary is a democracy with effective control and functioning security forces.
propositions.quote: Having canvassed the country conditions documents, the RAD finds that Hungary is a democracy in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds Hungary is a democracy with effective control and functioning security forces.

propositions.text: Refugee protection is surrogate protection invoked after unsuccessful state protection attempts.
propositions.quote: Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection to be invoked in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state.

propositions.text: Claimant must show they sought but could not obtain state protection or state could not be expected to provide it.
propositions.quote: To qualify for refugee status, a claimant must satisfy the Immigration and Refugee Board (Board) that he or she sought, but was unable to obtain, protection from their home state, or alternatively, that their home state, on an objective basis, could not be expected to provide protection.

propositions.text: Failure to pursue state protection in functioning democracy is usually fatal to refugee claim without compelling explanation.
propositions.quote: In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: Refugee protection is surrogate; failure to pursue state protection in democracy is fatal without good reason.

propositions.text: To rebut presumption of state protection, Appellant must provide clear and convincing evidence state protection is inadequate.
propositions.quote: To rebut the presumption of state protection, the Appellant must provide "clear and convincing" confirmation of the state's inability to protect its citizens.

propositions.text: Evidence must be reliable, probative, and satisfy balance of probabilities that state protection is inadequate.
propositions.quote: The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the RAD, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: State's serious efforts to protect citizens means mere failures do not rebut presumption of protection.
propositions.quote: Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.

propositions.text: Subjective reluctance to engage state does not rebut presumption of state protection.
propositions.quote: An Appellant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.

propositions.text: Doubting state protection effectiveness without testing it does not rebut presumption.
propositions.quote: Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant must provide clear, convincing, reliable evidence that state protection is inadequate; subjective doubts insufficient.

propositions.text: Appellant's burden of proof increases with level of democracy in state.
propositions.quote: An Appellant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the Appellant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.

propositions.text: In functioning democracies like Hungary, Appellant must show all reasonable steps taken to seek protection.
propositions.quote: In countries such as Hungary, the Appellant must do more than merely show that he went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. An Appellant must show that he has taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection...

propositions.text: Local failures do not mean state fails to protect unless part of broader pattern of refusal or inability.
propositions.quote: Local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.

propositions.text: No government guarantees perfect protection; less than perfect protection is not basis to find state unwilling or unable to protect.
propositions.quote: No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim...Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.

paragraphs.summary: In democracies like Hungary, Appellant must exhaust reasonable protection steps; imperfect protection does not mean state fails.

propositions.text: Federal Court decisions question state protection availability for Roma returning to Hungary and create uncertainty for this Board's analysis.
propositions.quote: recent decisions by the Federal Court have questioned whether state protection is available to members of the Roma community if they were to return to Hungary, and have thrown some uncertainty as to the manner in which this Board is to conduct a state protection analysis with respect to Roma citizens of Hungary.

propositions.text: Federal Court is divided on how to analyze state protection for Hungarian Roma claimants.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court is divided as to how best this analysis should take place.

propositions.text: Mudrak decision acknowledges division among Federal Court judges on state protection for Hungarian Roma claimants.
propositions.quote: It is well recognized that there is a division in the ranks of judges of the Federal Court on the issue of state protection, particularly as it applies to claimants from the Hungarian Roma community.

propositions.text: Mudrak decision quotes divergent Federal Court opinions on state protection for Roma community members.
propositions.quote: The court went on to highlight this division by quoting decisions from the Federal Court which provided divergent opinions on state protection for members of the Roma community.

propositions.text: Two decisions best illustrate the Federal Court's divided legal mindset on this issue.
propositions.quote: There are two decisions which best illustrate the divided legal mind set of the Federal Court on this issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Federal Court decisions show division and uncertainty about state protection for Roma in Hungary, citing Mudrak and two key decisions.

propositions.text: Moczo decision involved Hungarian Roma family seeking refugee protection based on discrimination and persecution.
propositions.quote: In that particular claim, the applicants are an extended family from Hungary. In 2010, they sought refugee protection in Canada based on their experiences of discrimination and persecution as members of the Roma community.

propositions.text: Applicants alleged attacks on their home including a concrete wall pushed onto roof and bricks thrown at house.
propositions.quote: In particular, they allege that their home was attacked by a group that pushed a concrete wall onto its roof. Later, someone threw bricks at the house.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Moczo decision where a Hungarian Roma family alleged attacks and sought refugee protection.

propositions.text: Federal Court allowed appeal, disagreed with Board's conclusion that applicants did not seek state protection reasonably.
propositions.quote: The Court did not agree with the Board's conclusion that the applicants had not made reasonable efforts to seek state protection.

propositions.text: Applicants approached police twice about bricks thrown; police did not report or act.
propositions.quote: The Board failed to take account of evidence showing that two of the applicants had approached the police on separate occasions to complain about bricks being thrown at their house. The police did not make a report; they simply said there was nothing they could do.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Federal Court in Moczo found applicants sought state protection but police failed to act.

propositions.text: Federal Court concluded state protection was unavailable due to police discrimination and failure to investigate violence against Roma.
propositions.quote: the Board concentrated on evidence relating to improvements not yet realized to the exclusion of the documentary evidence showing that Hungarian police often discriminate against and fail to investigate crimes of violence against the Roma.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Federal Court found state protection unavailable because police discriminated and failed to investigate violence against Roma.

propositions.text: Racz decision involved applicants attacked at home with stones thrown and father assaulted; police called but took limited action.
propositions.quote: In that the particular claim, the applicants: ...were at home when stones were thrown through their windows. Denes Csaba Racz, the father in the applicant family, ran out of the house to see what had happened but he was immediately kicked in his stomach and assaulted... The police said that there was not much they could do, but that they would patrol the area more often. They left without taking a report.

propositions.text: Applicants asked village Mayor for help; Mayor deferred to police.
propositions.quote: The applicants also asked the Mayor of their village to help them but he said the police would take care of things.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Racz decision where applicants were attacked, police took limited action, and Mayor deferred to police.

propositions.text: Federal Court dismissed appeal, found Board's decision on adequacy of state protection reasonable.
propositions.quote: I am unable to find, based on their submissions in this application, that the Board's decision that they did not establish the inadequacy of state protection is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Police response was adequate and comparable to Canadian police under similar circumstances.
propositions.quote: In fact, although not perfect, the response of the police to the applicants' complaints, given the specific circumstances of the assaults taken to the police, appears to have been adequate and in keeping with what Canadian police forces would be likely to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Federal Court in Racz found police response adequate and upheld the Board's decision.

propositions.text: Mudrak certified two questions; Federal Court of Appeal has not yet decided them.
propositions.quote: Although the Court in Mudrak certified two questions, the Federal Court of Appeal has yet to render a decision on the certified questions.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Mudrak certified questions remain undecided by the Federal Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: RAD must conclude on state protection for Roma in Hungary despite divergent Federal Court views.
propositions.quote: Given then this divergent view with respect to "clear and convincing" evidence, the RAD must attempt to come to some form of conclusion with respect to state protection for Roma in Hungary.

propositions.text: Sztojka decision states applicant bears evidentiary and legal burden to prove inadequate state protection on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: An applicant bears both an evidentiary and legal burden; she must introduce evidence of inadequate state protection and must convince the trier of fact that the evidence adduced establishes that the state protection is inadequate. The evidence will have sufficient probative value if it convinces the trier of fact on the balance of probabilities that the state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: Evidence must be relevant, reliable and convincing to meet burden of proof on state protection inadequacy.
propositions.quote: Therefore the evidence must be relevant, reliable and convincing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD must decide on state protection for Roma, guided by Sztojka requiring relevant, reliable, convincing evidence on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: State protection is not perfect in any country, including Hungary.
propositions.quote: The first principle is that protection provided by the state is not perfect. This applies not just to the country in question in this claim, Hungary, but to any other country.

propositions.text: Racz decision referenced Canadian police response as a comparison for adequacy of state protection.
propositions.quote: In the Racz decision quoted above, the court made a reference as to what Canadian forces would do under similar situations.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains state protection is imperfect everywhere and Racz compared Hungarian police to Canadian police.

propositions.text: Police are primarily responsible for state protection against violent attacks.
propositions.quote: The second legal principle which aids the RAD in determining whether clear and convincing evidence of a lack of state protection has been presented is that the police are primarily responsible for state protection against violent attacks.

propositions.text: Failure of one police officer or department to investigate does not alone prove no state protection.
propositions.quote: The failure of one police officer or one police department to investigate a crime does not, by itself, determine that there is no state protection.

propositions.text: Police not apprehending assailants or not pursuing complaints diligently does not mean state protection is inadequate.
propositions.quote: Just because the police did not apprehend the assailants in a particular incident, or that the Appellants' complaint was not pursued with the diligence that the Appellants would have preferred does not mean that state protection in their home country is not adequate.

propositions.text: Many factors may explain police failures; panel must assess if state protection was reasonably inadequate given circumstances.
propositions.quote: There may be many factors that could contribute to this, including lack of physical evidence, lack of suspects, higher priorities for the police, and lack of witnesses. It is open to the panel to determine if the state was unable to protect them, not in the absolute sense, but rather to a degree that was reasonable having regard to the circumstances of the Appellants.

propositions.text: Local police failures do not indicate no protection in the country as a whole.
propositions.quote: As the Federal Court has stated on numerous occasions, failures by local police to provide protection is not indicative of the fact that there is no protection in the country as a whole.

paragraphs.summary: The court states police are mainly responsible for protection; isolated police failures do not prove inadequate state protection overall.

propositions.text: RAD finds appellants have not rebutted presumption of state protection on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: the RAD finds that, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants have not rebutted the presumption of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellants failed to rebut presumption of state protection on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Appellants argue no state protection in Hungary due to Roma ethnicity.
propositions.quote: counsel for the Appellants argues that there is no state protection for the Appellants on account of their Roma ethnicity in Hungary.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue there is no state protection for Roma in Hungary.

propositions.text: Documentation shows widespread reports of intolerance, discrimination, and persecution of Roma in Hungary.
propositions.quote: there is information in the documentation... to indicate that there is widespread reporting of incidents of intolerance, discrimination and persecution of Romani individuals in Hungary.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges documentation reports widespread intolerance and persecution of Roma in Hungary.

propositions.text: Violent attacks against Roma continue, causing public concern and disputes about racially motivated crimes.
propositions.quote: Violent attacks against Roma continued, generating strong public concern and intense disputes as to the existence and scale of racially motivated crimes.

propositions.text: Human rights NGOs complain law enforcement reluctant to recognize racial motivation in crimes against Roma.
propositions.quote: Human rights NGOs complained that law enforcement authorities, prosecutors, and courts were reluctant to recognize racial motivation for many crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes ongoing violent attacks against Roma and NGO complaints about law enforcement reluctance to recognize racial motives.

propositions.text: Hungarian Guard and far-right groups held demonstrations inciting prejudice against Roma under guise of protecting Hungary.
propositions.quote: Hungarian Guard and other far-right organizations held demonstrations across the country with the goal of inciting 'prejudice' against the Roma.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports far-right groups held demonstrations inciting prejudice against Roma in Hungary.

propositions.text: Central government is motivated and willing to protect Roma but local implementation is sometimes ineffective.
propositions.quote: central government is motivated and willing to implement measures to protect the Roma, but these measures are not always implemented effectively at the local or municipal level.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Hungary's central government willing to protect Roma but local implementation is sometimes ineffective.

propositions.text: Despite inconsistencies, evidence suggests adequate state protection for Roma victims in Hungary and serious government efforts.
propositions.quote: there is adequate state protection in Hungary for Roma who are victims of crime, police abuse, discrimination or persecution, that Hungary is making serious efforts to address these problems, and that the police and government officials are both willing and able to protect victims.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence shows adequate state protection and serious efforts to protect Roma victims in Hungary.

propositions.text: Police still commit abuses against Roma but authorities are expected to take action and protect Roma.
propositions.quote: police do still commit abuses against people, including the Roma, but there is also evidence that indicates it is reasonable to expect authorities to take action in these cases, and that the police are capable of protecting Roma.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds police abuses occur but authorities are expected and capable of protecting Roma.

propositions.text: Roma face discrimination in education, employment, housing, social services, and public places in Hungary.
propositions.quote: Roma continue to face discrimination in education, employment, housing, and access to social services... denial of service in commercial establishments is almost exclusively experienced by the Roma.

propositions.text: Failures by local authorities to implement anti-discrimination laws contribute to Roma discrimination.
propositions.quote: Failures to act by local authorities, and in particular, failures in implementing centrally enacted legislation in conformity with the prohibition on discrimination, continue to lie at the heart of much of the discrimination experienced by Roma in daily life.

propositions.text: Hungary has initiatives addressing Roma issues in education, employment, housing, health, and political representation.
propositions.quote: Hungary has taken a number of initiatives relating to the situation of the Roma including, education, employment, housing, health, and political representation.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Roma discrimination in many areas and Hungary's initiatives to address these issues.

propositions.text: Roma minorities in Hungary can elect minority self-governments that organize cultural and educational affairs and participate in local government.
propositions.quote: Roma, like the other 12 official minorities, are entitled to elect their own minority self-governments (MSGs), which organize minority activities and handle cultural and educational affairs. The president of each MSG also has the right to attend and speak at local government assemblies.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Roma minorities in Hungary have elected self-governments with cultural and local government participation rights.

propositions.text: The Equal Treatment Authority provides direct redress for discrimination violations since 2005, with increasing complaints.
propositions.quote: There is also recourse to the Equal Treatment Authority who since 2005 has provided individuals with a direct avenue of redress for violations of the prohibition of discrimination in a variety of public and private law relationships.

propositions.text: Other remedies include compensation through courts and Parliamentary Commissioners for public authorities.
propositions.quote: There are also other remedies such as seeking compensation through the courts, or turning to one of the Parliamentary Commissioners where public authorities are concerned.

propositions.text: Roma Police Officers' Association allows Roma to file complaints, mostly about employment and police discrimination.
propositions.quote: There is also the Roma Police Officers' Association in Hungary, and Roma are able to file a complaint to the association. The complaints mostly concern discrimination in employment, discriminatory treatment and discrimination by law enforcement authorities or police officers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that the Equal Treatment Authority and other remedies address discrimination complaints, including those by Roma to the Police Officers' Association.

propositions.text: Appellants have access to various programs for assistance against discrimination.
propositions.quote: If the Appellants face discrimination, they have recourse to all of these programs for assistance should they need it.

propositions.text: Hungary has advanced minority protection systems and institutions for Roma integration.
propositions.quote: According to the Open Society Institute, Hungary has one of the most advanced systems for minority protection in the region.

propositions.text: Government institutions include Roma Integration Department and Council of Roma Integration coordinating social inclusion.
propositions.quote: The Hungarian Government lists a number of institutions within the state apparatus, including the Roma Integration Department within the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, the main government body responsible for Romani integration, and the Council of Roma Integration, a consultative, advisory body which coordinates measures between various ministries on the social inclusion of Roma.

propositions.text: Segregation of Roma students increased but government introduced measures to integrate them into mainstream education.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence indicates that segregation of Roma students has increased in the past decade, but at the same time, the government of Hungary has introduced numerous measures to integrate Roma students into mainstream education.

propositions.text: Minorities Ombudsman criticizes lack of monitoring and municipal resistance to investigations against segregation.
propositions.quote: the Minorities Ombudsman indicates that there is not enough monitoring of the programs and the municipalities resist against the investigations by the Ombudsman and courts, which are trying to stop school segregation.

propositions.text: Since 2003, education reforms and financial support programs target integration of disadvantaged students including Roma.
propositions.quote: A substantial reform of education, which included renewal of pedagogical methods, revision of legislation on education concerning multiple disadvantages and financial incentives, began in 2003.

propositions.text: Hungary implemented programs in 1,800 schools with a $40 million budget to fight segregation and dropout rates.
propositions.quote: Hungary implemented several programmes in 1,800 education institutions; the budget assigned for this purpose was about US $40 million.

propositions.text: Programs covered 300,000 pupils and 13,000 teachers by 2010.
propositions.quote: those programs "covered almost 300,000 pupils and reached approximately 13,000 teachers in 1,800 schools."

propositions.text: SROP 2007-2013 co-financed by EU supports equal opportunity programs for disadvantaged children.
propositions.quote: Hungary's Social Renewal Operation Programme (SROP) 2007-2013, co-financed by the European Union, includes the Promotion of Implementation of Equal Opportunities Programmes that are designed to improve the situation of children with multiple disadvantages.

propositions.text: SROP supports teacher training, methodological development, and extracurricular activities for informal learning.
propositions.quote: SROP co-ordinates and supports programs related to the development of methodological documents, teacher training courses, and extracurricular activities that encourage opportunities of informal learning.

propositions.text: Open Society Foundations praises SROP as a positive policy example for Roma integration.
propositions.quote: The Open Society Foundations (OSF), an international organization that works to build democracies with accountable governments and implements initiatives at the local level in its study on Roma integration strategies, points out that the SROP project is a positive policy example.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Hungary has advanced minority protection, education reforms, and programs supporting Roma integration despite some segregation issues.

propositions.text: Most ministries and county labor centers have special officers for Romani affairs.
propositions.quote: Most ministries and county labour affairs centers had special officers for Romani affairs focused on the needs of the Romani community.

propositions.text: Ministry of National Resources offers financial incentives to integrate Romani children and reintegrate those in remedial programs.
propositions.quote: The Ministry of National Resources continued to offer financial incentives to encourage schools to integrate Romani and non-Romani children in the same classrooms and to reintegrate Roma inappropriately placed in remedial programs.

propositions.text: Ministry finances infrastructure development in Romani communities.
propositions.quote: The Ministry also operated a program to finance infrastructure development in Romani communities.

propositions.text: Prime minister appointed Zoltan Balog as state secretary for social inclusion to coordinate Roma issues.
propositions.quote: The prime minister named Zoltan Balog as state secretary for social inclusion, charged with coordinating government efforts to address Roma issues.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes government ministries have officers and programs for Roma integration and social inclusion coordination.

propositions.text: Ministry of Public Administration and Justice runs anti-discrimination legal aid network for Roma.
propositions.quote: The Ministry of Public Administration and Justice (formerly the Ministry of Justice and Law Enforcement) operated an anti-discrimination legal service network that provided free legal aid to Roma in cases where they encountered ethnic discrimination.

propositions.text: Human rights NGOs criticize the network's offices are in large cities, inaccessible to poor Roma in villages.
propositions.quote: Human rights NGOs lamented that the lawyers' offices were located in the larger cities, rendering them inaccessible to those Roma living in deep poverty in small villages.

propositions.text: HCLU received reports that the network's lawyers rejected some Romani cases.
propositions.quote: HCLU received reports that the network's lawyers rejected some Romani cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Ministry's legal aid network for Roma faces accessibility and case rejection issues per NGOs and HCLU reports.

propositions.text: Since 2009, cities must include desegregation plans to get EU and government urban and education funds.
propositions.quote: Since January 2009, in order to apply for EU and government funds for urban rehabilitation and public education projects, every city must attach to its proposal, a desegregation plan outlining planned actions to eradicate segregation in housing and public education.

propositions.text: Government opened 200 public administration positions for Romani college graduates; 165 passed exams, 66 placed.
propositions.quote: The government opened 200 positions in public administration for Romani college graduates. By year's end, 165 applicants had passed the mandatory civil servant entry exam and 66 were placed in various national and county government offices.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Hungary requires desegregation plans for funding and has placed Roma graduates in public administration.

propositions.text: No evidence shows Hungarian authorities actively prevented Appellants from employment in their professions.
propositions.quote: there is no evidence before the RAD to demonstrate that the Hungarian authorities took active steps to prevent the Appellants from obtaining employment in their respective professions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence that Hungarian authorities actively prevented the Appellants from employment.

propositions.text: Federal Court in Balaz recognized Roma face discrimination, sometimes amounting to persecution.
propositions.quote: As the Federal Court has stated in Balaz, "...it is recognized that people of Roma ethnicity are the subject of discriminatory acts and, in some cases, that discrimination is considered persecution..."

propositions.text: Discrimination in Hungary does not automatically mean lack of state protection for Roma.
propositions.quote: the very fact that discrimination does exist in Hungary does not, de facto, translate into a lack of state protection.

propositions.text: Comparison to discrimination against Canada's First Nations, who still receive state protection.
propositions.quote: I am sure that members of Canada's First Nations would also readily cite attitudes of discrimination against them here in our own country of Canada. And that may well be true. However, this does not mean that Canada does not provide protection for members of its First Nations.

propositions.text: Discrimination against Roma in Hungary does not mean no state protection or no requirement to seek it before refuge.
propositions.quote: The fact that Roma are discriminated against in Hungary does not mean that there is never any state protection for them or that they are not required to seek that protection prior to seeking refuge in another country.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Federal Court recognizing Roma discrimination but finds discrimination alone does not negate state protection in Hungary.

propositions.text: No fixed template exists to determine if Roma Appellants rebut presumption of state protection; cases are fact-specific.
propositions.quote: There is no boiler template for determining whether the Appellants of Roma ethnicity have rebutted the presumption of state protection. Each case must be determined on its individual facts and circumstances.

propositions.text: Based on evidence and Federal Court decision in Kotai, not all Roma can avoid seeking state protection before refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the country conditions do not suggest that the situation is so bleak that all Roma, regardless of their particular circumstances, should not be expected to make reasonable efforts to seek state protection before seeking refugee protection in another country.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no fixed test exists; relying on Kotai, Roma must generally seek state protection before refugee claims.

propositions.text: Appellants bear burden to prove state unwillingness or inability to protect with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the Appellant to provide clear and convincing evidence that the state is either unwilling or unable to provide him with adequate protection.

propositions.text: RPD need not prove state protection exists; claimant must rebut presumption on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The RPD is not obliged to provide proof that the state can offer its citizens effective protection, rather the claimant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the RPD, on a balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Appellants must prove lack of state protection; RPD presumes protection unless rebutted.

propositions.text: Whether adequate state protection is available to Appellants in Hungary upon return.
propositions.quote: the issue before it was whether adequate state protection is and would be available to the Appellants in their home country of Hungary should they return.

propositions.text: States presumed capable of protecting nationals; Appellants may rebut with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: While states are presumed to be capable of protecting their nationals, it is open, according to the law, for the Appellants to rebut the presumption of protection with clear and convincing evidence that adequate protection would not reasonably be forthcoming.

propositions.text: Appellants have not rebutted presumption of state protection; appeal must fail.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on the evidence, that the Appellants have not rebutted that presumption and, as the issue of state protection is equally applicable to claims based on sections 96 and 97, the Appeal must fail.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the issue is state protection availability; Appellants failed to rebut presumption, so appeal fails.

propositions.text: RAD agrees with RPD's state protection and credibility findings.
propositions.quote: The RAD has assessed the entirety of the evidence and I have determined that I arrived at the same conclusion as the RPD did in its decision regarding the Sate Protection finding. In regard to the credibility findings made by the RPD, the RAD will recognize and respect those RPD findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the RPD's findings on state protection and credibility.

propositions.text: State protection issue is determinative; no need to consider other grounds raised by Appellant.
propositions.quote: As such, the issue of State Protection is determinative in disposing of this appeal, and it is not necessary for the RAD to consider the other grounds raised by the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes state protection issue decides the appeal; other grounds need not be considered.

propositions.text: RAD confirms RPD decision that Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision denying refugee protection to the Appellants.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The appeal is therefore, dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.
